coherence.reasons: X's governing thought says the margin reaches 3.0% by FY2028, but its own backup shows this holds only before the 2027 wage rise (2.5% with it, 2.96% with reserves). The 3.02% also counts all nine store exits, while the recommendation defers three of them to a later vote. Its promotions lever is sized as a full chain-wide return to the FY2023 mix, yet the text says depth stays in ValuMart areas. Y's governing thought (about 2.6% on firm levers, a prepared second wave to reach 3.0%) matches its bridge, options table, ranges and checkpoint. The wage step and delivery rate rise sit in Y's baseline, so the summary, the gap ($35.6M) and the lever totals tie together. Y's one loose point is the slide title saying the plan 'reaches 3.0%', which is true only with the second wave.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the 8% cut and lead with promotions, shrink, delivery repricing and lease-expiry exits, which is the answer key's preferred shape. Y weighs the alternatives more fully. It compares three options on margin, one-time cost, covenant and commitments, and keeps click-and-collect-only as a fallback that needs the owners' consent. It haircuts the promotions gain by 25% for lost traffic, phases FY2026 to show about $5M of covenant headroom, budgets about $17M of one-time cost against the $25M cap, and sets a mid-FY2027 trigger. Y also admits the firm levers fall short of 3.0%. X treats closing delivery as out of scope, gives no FY2026 phasing (it only compares full run-rate with the $4.7M need), does not budget one-time costs beyond the $7.5M lease exit, and counts no lost volume from the promotions reset. X's reserve logic for the wage rise is sensible but still lands just under target. Y's vendor-funding and contract-reduction levers are speculative, but they are flagged and ranged.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: the bridge components, 13% for labor, the $10.4M e-commerce drag, about $12.34 lost per delivery, $6.6M for nine closures, and the fulfilment rebuild. X's weaker inferences are these: it scales the whole 0.5 pp shrink rise to an 8% cut ($10.0M) and then headlines 'Draft misses $20M' on that admitted upper bound; it assumes moving hours with total hours flat takes the whole fleet to the best quartile's 2.3% shrink at no cost; and it sizes the promotions reset at the full 5 pp with no volume loss while exempting ValuMart stores. Y uses a more measured shrink clawback ($3.8–7.5M) and nets $1.5M of reinvested hours. It tests the category team's claim quantitatively (break-even of 2.3 points of promo share, plus the correlation caveat). It reconciles the e-commerce team's 6.1% to −$0.5M and then to −8.2%, and it flags survey, correlation and pro-rata caveats. Y's weak spots are assumed allowances, the vendor-funding sizing, the 5% contract reduction, and an ambiguous base for the 3% labor lever. Most of these are labelled as team estimates.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's wage hypothesis. Each shows labor is about 13% of the decline, that fewer hours per sale absorbed most of the wage rise, and that low-labor stores have higher shrink; each replaces the across-the-board cut and the e-commerce freeze. Y goes a little further. It decomposes wage (+1.11 pts) against productivity (−0.77 pts), explains why the dollar view misled management, carries the draft plan through to FY2028 (about 1.1%), and keeps a targeted labor reduction with the shrink risk sized. It also concedes the draft could meet the covenant on paper. X's rejection leans on an upper-bound shrink estimate to claim the draft misses the covenant, which overstates the case. Its reserve cut in the best-staffed stores, held until shrink is stable, is a sound handling of the labor lever.

overall.reasons: Both documents reach a defensible, sized plan built on the right diagnosis. Y would serve the CEO better. Its baseline includes the known 2027 wage step, and it is candid that the firm levers reach about 2.6% and need a second wave. It gives ranges, FY2026 phasing against the covenant, a one-time cost budget, an options comparison with a fallback, and triggers. X is clear and largely accurate, but its headline 3.0% depends on optimistic sizing (full promotions reversal with no volume loss, fleet shrink at best-quartile level from reallocation alone, all nine exits) and leaves the wage rise out of the base case. Its claim that the draft misses the covenant rests on an upper-bound estimate.
